```{r load-all, include=FALSE}
# The pipeline writes one indicator-level panel (with raw and scaled values
# in the same file), one scores file, and one trajectories file. Metadata
# like module, unit, direction, and source lives in the indicators registry
# and is joined on as needed — it isn't duplicated across panel rows.
panel_raw    <- read_csv("data/output/country_year_indicators.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
scores_raw   <- read_csv("data/output/country_year_scores.csv",     show_col_types = FALSE)
trajectories <- read_csv("data/output/country_trajectories.csv",    show_col_types = FALSE)
indicators   <- read_csv("config/indicators.csv",                   show_col_types = FALSE)

# Renormalised weights, used in a couple of display chunks below.
weights <- indicators |>
  select(module, indicator, weight) |>
  group_by(module) |>
  mutate(weight = weight / sum(weight)) |>
  ungroup()

# Restrict all in-notebook analysis to a consistent window. The indicator
# panel contains both raw values and scaled values in the same rows, so
# `panel` and `normalized` here are the same table — the two names are
# kept because different sections of this notebook talk about the data
# either as the raw-value panel or as the scaled panel.
panel      <- panel_raw |> filter(year >= ANALYSIS_START_YEAR)
normalized <- panel
scores     <- scores_raw |> filter(year >= ANALYSIS_START_YEAR)

latest_year <- max(scores$year)
```

# A note for the reader

This notebook is meant for someone who has **never seen this project
before** and who is **not a data scientist or statistician**. It does
not assume you know what a "data panel," a "percentile rank," or a
"weighted average" is. Wherever a piece of jargon appears, it is
introduced in plain language first, and every chart is followed by a
plain-English reading of what it does and does not say.

The notebook is long, but it is built up gradually:

- **Part A** explains what this project is trying to do, what the data
  is, where it comes from, and what each piece of it means.
- **Part B** walks through, step by step with real numbers, how a
  single measurement turns into the kind of score the rest of the
  notebook uses.
- **Part C** is the actual exploration — looking at coverage, sanity
  checking the inputs, examining how the pieces fit together, and
  describing what the world looks like in this dataset.
- **Part D** is honest about everything the model cannot do, and what
  would have to change for it to do those things.

If you only have a few minutes, read Part A, skim the headings of
Part B, and then jump to **Section C5** ("Where is the world
heading?"), which is the most direct payoff of the whole pipeline.

---

# Part A — What is this, and what is the data?

# A1. What is this project trying to do?

The Life Projection project is, at its heart, an attempt to build a
**numerical portrait of every country in the world, in every year
since 2000**. The idea is that if you can describe each country with
a consistent set of measurements — how healthy people are, how rich
the country is, how free the political system is, how stable the
society is, and so on — then you can do useful things with that
portrait:

1. **Compare countries to each other** in a structured way.
2. **Watch how each country changes over time.**
3. **Identify which countries are improving, deteriorating, or
   stagnating** on each dimension.

The eventual ambition — explicitly *not* what this notebook does — is
to use that picture as scaffolding for thinking about how a person's
life might unfold given the country they live in. That is a long way
off. This notebook is just about whether the picture itself is
reasonable.

## What "the data" is, in one sentence

The data is a giant spreadsheet where **every row is one country, in
one year, on one measurement**. So if there are about 200 countries,
25 years of data (2000 through today), and 40 different measurements,
you end up with on the order of 200 × 25 × 40 = **200,000 rows**.

That's it. That's the whole dataset. The rest of the project is just
ways of turning that long thin spreadsheet into something
interpretable — averages, rankings, trends, summaries.

---

# A2. Where does the data come from?

Every number in this project comes from one of two free, public,
internationally-respected sources. We do not collect any data
ourselves; we are downloading what these institutions have already
gathered and published.

## A2.1 The World Bank

The [World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/) maintains the largest
publicly available database of country-level statistics in the world.
Most of its numbers are not collected by the World Bank itself. Instead,
the World Bank acts as a **clearinghouse**: it gathers data that
individual countries' national statistics agencies produce (the U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics, India's National Sample Survey
Organisation, Germany's Destatis, etc.), standardizes the formatting
and definitions across countries, and republishes them through a free
public web service called an **API**.

Concretely, in this project, the script `01_fetch_data.R` makes a
request to a World Bank web address that looks like:

```
https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN
```

The code at the end of that URL — `SP.DYN.LE00.IN` — is the World
Bank's internal name for "Life expectancy at birth, total (years)."
The server responds with a long list of (country, year, value)
records, which we then save to disk as a CSV file.

**What the World Bank typically gives us** in this project:

- Economic indicators: GDP per person, GDP growth, inflation,
  unemployment, savings rate, government debt
- Demographic indicators: birth rate, life expectancy, urbanization
- Health: infant mortality, hospital beds, vaccination rates
- Technology: internet users, mobile phone subscriptions
- Climate-adjacent: CO2 emissions per person, energy use per person

**How was this data originally collected?** It varies enormously by
indicator and by country. A few examples to make this concrete:

- *Life expectancy* comes from death certificates and population
  censuses. A country's statistical office calculates, "If a baby
  born today experienced the death rates we observed at every age
  this year, how long would they live on average?" The World Bank
  then publishes that single number per country, per year.
- *Internet users (% of population)* comes from household surveys
  conducted by the International Telecommunication Union (a UN
  agency) and by national statistics offices, asking, "Has anyone
  in this household used the internet in the last three months?"
- *Inflation (consumer price index)* comes from monthly price
  collection visits to thousands of shops in each country by
  government statisticians who literally write down what a loaf
  of bread, a litre of milk, etc. cost, and then aggregate.
- *CO2 emissions per person* comes from energy-use data and
  factory output data, multiplied by chemical conversion factors,
  then divided by the country's population.

This range matters because **data quality varies wildly**. A rich
country with a long-established statistics agency (Germany, Japan)
produces a very different quality of inflation number from a country
in active conflict (Syria, Yemen) where statisticians can't safely
visit shops. The numbers all *look* the same when you put them in a
spreadsheet — but they are not the same.

## A2.2 Our World In Data (OWID)

[Our World In Data](https://ourworldindata.org) is a research project
based at the University of Oxford that does something similar to the
World Bank but for **academic and specialty datasets**. Where the
World Bank focuses on official government statistics, OWID republishes
datasets that come from research institutes, academic projects, and
international agencies that don't have their own public API.

In this project, OWID is the source for two important things:

1. **V-Dem democracy indices.** V-Dem ("Varieties of Democracy") is
   a research project at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden. They
   send detailed questionnaires to country experts — typically
   political scientists who specialize in a particular country —
   asking 470 questions about the political situation in that country
   in that year. Are elections clean? Can opposition parties operate?
   Does the judiciary actually act independently of the government?
   Each question is answered on a numeric scale, and the answers are
   aggregated into composite indices like *liberal democracy index*,
   *electoral democracy index*, *rule of law*, and so on. These are
   the most rigorous quantitative measurements of governance we have.
2. **Specialty climate, health, and emissions data** that the World
   Bank does not publish, or publishes less reliably.

OWID is fetched in the same script (`01_fetch_data.R`), through a
different URL pattern. Each OWID dataset has a "slug" name and is
downloaded as a CSV.

## A2.3 What we are *not* using (and why it matters)

There is one important source that we wanted but do not have:
**ACLED** (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data). ACLED is the gold
standard for fine-grained data on political violence — battle deaths,
protests, riots, attacks on civilians — but it requires an
institutional research license that this project does not have. As a
substitute, we use V-Dem's "rule of law" and "control of corruption"
indices as proxies for stability, which is **not the same thing** as
direct measures of violence and is one of the model's most important
limitations.

A free alternative, **UCDP** (Uppsala Conflict Data Program), is
downloadable as CSVs without an API key and could be added as a
follow-up to repair this gap.

---

# A3. What is the structure of the data?

This section is hands-on. We are going to look at literal rows of the
actual data we use, because that is the fastest way to develop a
feel for what's in here.

## A3.1 One row at a time

After all the downloading and combining, the master table looks like
this. Here are the first ten rows of the data for the United States:

```{r show-raw-rows}
panel |>
  filter(country_iso3 == "USA") |>
  left_join(indicators |> select(indicator, unit, source), by = "indicator") |>
  arrange(year, indicator) |>
  head(10) |>
  select(country_iso3, year, indicator, value, unit, source) |>
  kable(caption = "First 10 rows of the data, for the USA. Each row is one country, one year, one measurement. (unit and source come from the indicator registry — they are properties of the indicator, not the observation, so they aren't repeated in the panel itself.)")
```

Reading the first row: in the year **2000**, the **United States**
had a value for the indicator **`co2_per_capita`** measured in the
unit **tonnes**. That single number came from **OWID**'s emissions
dataset. The next row is the same year, same country, a different
indicator. And so on.

This format — one measurement per row — is sometimes called **long
format**. It is the format that scales: adding a new indicator means
adding more rows, not new columns. Tables like this can have hundreds
of thousands of rows but only six or seven columns.

The full panel in this run contains
**`r format(nrow(panel), big.mark = ",")` rows** across
**`r n_distinct(panel$country_iso3)` countries** and
**`r n_distinct(panel$indicator)` indicators**, from
**`r min(panel$year)`** to **`r max(panel$year)`**.

## A3.2 What identifies a country?

You may have noticed the column `country_iso3` instead of just a
country name. Country names are a *mess* in data work — is it
"Republic of Korea," "South Korea," "Korea, Rep.," "Korea (Republic
of)"? Different sources use different conventions, which makes
joining tables painful.

To get around this, every country in the world has an **ISO 3166-1
alpha-3 code**: a three-letter identifier that is the same everywhere.

```{r iso-examples}
tibble::tribble(
  ~country,                ~iso3,
  "United States",         "USA",
  "Germany",               "DEU",
  "Japan",                 "JPN",
  "China",                 "CHN",
  "India",                 "IND",
  "Brazil",                "BRA",
  "South Africa",          "ZAF",
  "United Kingdom",        "GBR",
  "Republic of Korea",     "KOR",
  "Democratic Rep. Congo", "COD"
) |>
  kable(caption = "Country names are inconsistent across sources; ISO3 codes are not.")
```

Throughout this notebook, when you see codes like `USA` or `DEU`,
those are countries.

## A3.3 What is an "indicator"?

An **indicator** is just our internal name for one measurable thing —
"life expectancy at birth," "GDP per person in constant 2015 US
dollars," "share of population with internet access," and so on.

Each indicator has a small profile recorded in a configuration file
called `indicators.csv`, which tells the pipeline:

- which source to fetch it from (World Bank or OWID),
- what the source's internal name for it is,
- which **module** it belongs to (more on modules in a moment),
- what unit it's measured in,
- whether higher numbers are better or worse,
- and how much weight it should carry inside its module.

Here are a few example rows from that configuration:

```{r indicator-config-sample}
indicators |>
  filter(indicator %in% c("life_expectancy", "gdp_per_capita_ppp",
                          "infant_mortality", "co2_per_capita",
                          "liberal_democracy_index", "internet_users_share")) |>
  select(module, indicator, source, source_id, unit, direction, weight) |>
  arrange(module) |>
  kable(caption = "A few example indicator definitions, including their within-module weights.")
```

That `direction` column matters a lot. For something like life
expectancy, **higher is better**. For something like infant mortality,
**lower is better** — a country with infant mortality of 3 per 1,000
births is doing better than one at 50 per 1,000. Later in the pipeline,
when we standardize all indicators onto a common scale, the
`lower_is_better` ones get *flipped* so that "higher = better"
everywhere. This makes module scores interpretable.

The `weight` column is used much later, in **Step B4**, when
individual indicator scores are combined into module-level
scorecards. Some indicators are considered more central to their
module than others (life expectancy gets more weight than hospital
beds inside the health module, for example), and the weight column
encodes that judgement. Weights inside a module can be written on
any convenient scale — the pipeline renormalises them to sum to 1
before averaging.

## A3.4 What is a "module"?

40+ individual indicators is too many for a human to look at all at
once. So we group them into **eight thematic modules**:

```{r module-overview}
indicators |>
  count(module, name = "n_indicators") |>
  arrange(desc(n_indicators)) |>
  kable(caption = "The eight modules and how many indicators each contains.")
```

You can think of each module as a **scorecard subject** for a
country, the way a school report card has subjects (Math, English,
Science). The eight subjects here are:

| Module | What it tries to measure | Example indicators |
|---|---|---|
| **economy** | How the economy is doing | GDP per person, growth, inflation, debt |
| **labor** | Quality of the job market | Unemployment, labor force participation |
| **health** | Population health | Life expectancy, infant mortality, hospital capacity |
| **demographics** | Population structure | Birth rate, urbanization, age structure |
| **rights** | Political and civil rights | V-Dem democracy and rights indices |
| **stability** | Governance and rule of law | V-Dem rule-of-law and corruption indices |
| **climate** | Environmental footprint | CO2 per person, energy intensity |
| **technology** | Technological development | Internet, mobile, R&D spending |

The full list of every indicator and which module it belongs to is
shown in **Section C1.1**.

## A3.5 So what does one country look like overall?

Putting all the pieces together: for the United States in the year
2023, the pipeline holds something like 35 individual measurements,
spread across the eight modules. Here is a sample of what the USA's
data looks like in 2023:

```{r usa-2023}
panel |>
  filter(country_iso3 == "USA", year == max(year[country_iso3 == "USA"])) |>
  left_join(indicators |> select(indicator, module, unit), by = "indicator") |>
  arrange(module, indicator) |>
  select(module, indicator, value, unit) |>
  head(15) |>
  kable(caption = "Sample of the most-recent year of USA data, showing how indicators slot into modules.")
```

Every other country gets the same treatment, every year from 2000
onward, subject to whether the data was actually reported.

# Part B — From raw data to finished scores, traced step by step

This section is the "show your work" section. We are going to take
**one country and one indicator** and follow them all the way from
the moment the World Bank's server sends us a number, to the moment
that number becomes part of the United States' final scorecard.

If you only read one part of this notebook to understand how the
pipeline actually works, read this section.

# B1. Step 1 — The raw response from the source

The pipeline starts by making a web request to the World Bank API.
When we ask for life expectancy data, the server replies with
something that looks roughly like this (simplified for readability):

```
{
  "countryiso3code": "USA",
  "date": "2022",
  "value": 77.4280487804878,
  "indicator": { "id": "SP.DYN.LE00.IN", "value": "Life expectancy at birth" }
}
{
  "countryiso3code": "USA",
  "date": "2021",
  "value": 76.3329268292683,
  "indicator": { "id": "SP.DYN.LE00.IN", "value": "Life expectancy at birth" }
}
... (and so on, for every country and every year)
```

This is **JSON** — a common format for data on the web. The pipeline
parses it, throws away the metadata it doesn't need, and saves a
small CSV with just three columns:

```{r raw-csv-example, echo=FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~country_iso3, ~year, ~value,
  "USA",         2020,  77.000,
  "USA",         2021,  76.333,
  "USA",         2022,  77.428,
  "DEU",         2020,  81.100,
  "DEU",         2021,  80.900,
  "DEU",         2022,  80.700,
  "JPN",         2020,  84.620,
  "JPN",         2021,  84.530,
  "JPN",         2022,  84.020,
  "...",         NA,    NA
) |>
  kable(caption = "What the raw CSV looks like for one indicator (life expectancy). One row per country-year.")
```

There is now one such CSV file on disk for **every indicator** —
about 40 of them in this project. That is what "fetching the raw
data" amounts to.

# B2. Step 2 — Combining all indicators into one panel

Each of the 40 raw CSV files contains the same three columns
(`country_iso3`, `year`, `value`) but for a different measurement.
The next step (in `02_combine_process.R`) is to stack them all
together, tagging each row with which indicator it represents.

The result is a long thin table with just four columns:
`country_iso3`, `year`, `indicator`, and `value`. Other properties
of an indicator (which module it belongs to, what unit it's in, what
direction is "better," where the number came from) all live in the
indicator registry — `config/indicators.csv` — and get joined onto
the panel only when needed. That keeps the panel slim and avoids
repeating the same metadata across ~120,000 rows.

After this step the data, joined with the relevant metadata for
display, looks like this:

```{r combined-example}
panel |>
  filter(country_iso3 == "USA", year == 2020,
         indicator %in% c("life_expectancy", "gdp_per_capita_ppp",
                          "infant_mortality", "internet_users_share",
                          "co2_per_capita")) |>
  left_join(indicators |> select(indicator, module, unit), by = "indicator") |>
  arrange(indicator) |>
  select(country_iso3, year, indicator, value, unit, module) |>
  kable(caption = "After combining: one row per country-year-indicator. Module and unit come from the indicator registry — they're properties of the indicator, not the observation, so they live in indicators.csv and get joined on when needed.")
```

Five separate downloaded files have become five rows of one big
spreadsheet. Multiply this by all 200 countries and all 25 years and
all 40 indicators, and you get the master panel — about
`r format(round(nrow(panel)/1000)*1000, big.mark = ",")` rows in
this run.

# B3. Step 3 — Why raw values cannot be averaged directly

Here is the central problem this project has to solve:

> **You cannot meaningfully average life expectancy (a number around
> 80) with GDP per person (a number around 60,000) with the rule of
> law index (a number between 0 and 1).** They are in totally
> different units and on totally different scales.

If you just took the average, GDP per person would completely
dominate, and the answer would be roughly "GDP per person divided
by the number of indicators." The other measurements would be lost.

To combine indicators into a sensible score, we first have to put
them on a **common scale**. The pipeline uses two different ways of
doing this, and computes both for every measurement.

## B3.1 Method 1 — Where do you rank against everyone *this year*?

The first method is called `pct_global` in the data. It asks: **In
this specific year, where does this country rank against all other
countries on this specific indicator?**

The result is a number from 0 to 100, where:

- 0  means you are the worst country in the world this year on this measure
- 50 means you are exactly in the middle
- 100 means you are the best country in the world this year on this measure

This is called a **percentile rank**. It is the same logic as a
child's height percentile at a pediatrician's office: "90th
percentile for height" means 90% of children that age are shorter.

**A worked example.** Let's say in 2022 there are 180 countries with
life expectancy data, and the United States' life expectancy of
77.4 years ranks 35th from the top (well behind Japan, Switzerland,
Singapore, etc., but ahead of most of the world). Then USA's
`pct_global` for life expectancy that year would be:

```
(180 - 35) / 180 × 100 = 80.6
```

So the USA scores about **81 out of 100** on life expectancy
*relative to the rest of the world in 2022*.

**Why is this useful?** It tells you about your country's *position
in the global pecking order*. A score of 80 means "I'm doing better
than 80% of countries this year." That's intuitive and useful.

**Why is this not enough?** Imagine that next year, *every country
in the world* gets dramatically less healthy — life expectancy drops
by 5 years everywhere. The USA would still rank 35th out of 180,
and would still get a `pct_global` of 80. The score wouldn't move,
even though the world got worse. **Percentile ranks can't show
global movement** — if everyone moves together, the rankings stay
the same.

## B3.2 Method 2 — Where do you sit against the all-time global scale?

The second method is called `pct_fixed`. Instead of comparing you to
the other countries *this year*, it compares your value to the
**all-time range** that this indicator has ever taken across all
countries since 2000.

Specifically:

```
pct_fixed = (your value − all-time global minimum) /
            (all-time global maximum − all-time global minimum)
            × 100
```

This is called **min-max scaling**. It also produces a number from
0 to 100, but the meaning is different:

- 0   means you match the all-time worst on this indicator
- 100 means you match the all-time best on this indicator
- 50  means you are exactly halfway between the worst and best

**A worked example.** Life expectancy across all countries since
2000 ranges from about 38 years (worst, in a country during a
catastrophic period) to about 85 years (best, places like Japan and
Monaco in recent years). The USA's 77.4 years in 2022 would be:

```
(77.4 − 38) / (85 − 38) × 100  =  83.8
```

So the USA scores **about 84 out of 100** on the all-time global
scale.

**Why is this useful?** Unlike `pct_global`, this version *can*
detect global movement. If life expectancy collapses worldwide, the
denominator stays fixed at the historical range, and everyone's
score genuinely falls.

**Why is this not enough either?** It is vulnerable to **extreme
outliers**. If one country has CO2 emissions per person of 60 tonnes
(huge) while almost everyone else is between 0 and 15 tonnes, then
the "100" anchor sits way out at 60, and everyone below 15 ends up
crushed into a tiny range near 0. We will see this exact problem
hit several indicators in **Section C2**.

The pipeline computes **both** scaled versions for every
measurement. Different questions need different scales.

## B3.3 Handling "lower is better" indicators

One more subtlety. Some indicators are good when they go down
(infant mortality, inflation, CO2 emissions per person) and some
are good when they go up (life expectancy, GDP per person).

When we scale them, we want **higher = better in every case**,
because otherwise averaging them is incoherent. So for the
"lower is better" ones, we flip the score:

```
flipped_score = 100 − original_score
```

That is what the `direction` field in the indicator configuration
controls. After the flip, **a score of 80 always means "doing well"**
regardless of whether the underlying indicator was infant mortality
or life expectancy.

## B3.4 What the data looks like after Step 3

So now every original row has gained two new columns. Here is the
USA in 2020 again, this time with the scaled values:

```{r normalized-example}
normalized |>
  filter(country_iso3 == "USA", year == 2020,
         indicator %in% c("life_expectancy", "gdp_per_capita_ppp",
                          "infant_mortality", "internet_users_share",
                          "co2_per_capita")) |>
  left_join(indicators |> select(indicator, direction), by = "indicator") |>
  arrange(indicator) |>
  select(country_iso3, year, indicator, value, direction, pct_global, pct_fixed) |>
  mutate(across(c(pct_global, pct_fixed), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  kable(caption = "After scaling: every raw value has both a per-year ranking (pct_global) and an all-time-scale value (pct_fixed). Both are 0–100 with higher = better.")
```

Each of these scaled scores is now directly comparable across
indicators. A `pct_fixed` of 80 on life expectancy and a `pct_fixed`
of 80 on internet access both mean "doing 80% of the way from the
all-time global worst to the all-time global best." They can now be
averaged together meaningfully.

# B4. Step 4 — Combining indicators into module scores

Now that all indicators are on the same 0–100 scale, we can combine
them into the eight module scorecards.

For each module, the pipeline takes a **weighted average** of its
indicator scores. The weights live in the same `indicators.csv`
registry described in A3.3 — each indicator has a `weight` column
saying how much it should count inside its module. Some indicators
are considered more central to a module than others, so they count
more. The pipeline renormalises the per-module weights so they sum
to 1 before averaging, which means you can write the raw weights on
any convenient scale.

For example, the **health** module might be weighted like this
(values shown are proportions that sum to 1.0):

```{r show-weights-health}
weights |>
  filter(module == "health") |>
  arrange(desc(weight)) |>
  mutate(weight = round(weight, 3)) |>
  kable(caption = "Example: weights for indicators inside the 'health' module. They sum to 1.0.")
```

For a given country and year, the health module score is computed
as:

```
health_score = (life_expectancy_score × weight1) +
               (infant_mortality_score × weight2) +
               (hospital_beds_score × weight3) + ...
```

This is repeated for all eight modules.

**One important detail — missing data.** Not every country reports
every indicator every year. If a country is missing, say, the
"hospital beds per 1,000 people" measurement, the pipeline does not
treat it as zero (which would be wrong). Instead, it computes the
weighted average **only over the indicators that are present**, and
records a `coverage` number that tells you what fraction of the
module's expected indicators were available. A health score
computed from 5 out of 7 expected indicators has `coverage = 0.71`
and is more uncertain than one computed from 7 out of 7.

After this step, the data is now much shorter — one row per country,
per year, per module. Here is the USA's full set of 2020 module
scores:

```{r usa-scores-2020}
scores |>
  filter(country_iso3 == "USA", year == 2020) |>
  arrange(desc(score_pct_fixed)) |>
  select(country_iso3, year, module, score_pct_fixed, score_pct_global,
         contributing_count, expected_count, coverage) |>
  mutate(across(c(score_pct_fixed, score_pct_global, coverage), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  kable(caption = "The United States' eight module scores for 2020. coverage = how many of the module's expected indicators were available.")
```

This is, in compact form, the United States' "world model" entry
for the year 2020.

# B5. Step 5 — Trajectories: where is the country heading?

Module scores tell you where a country *is* in a given year. But the
more interesting question is often *where it is going*. The final
step of the pipeline computes a trajectory summary for every
country and module.

For each (country, module), we look at the last 5 years of scores
and ask:

1. **Level**: what is the most recent score?
2. **Trend**: is it going up or down, and how fast?
3. **Volatility**: is it stable, or jumping around?

The trend is computed by drawing a straight line through the last
five yearly scores and reading off its slope. (For readers familiar
with statistics, this is an ordinary least squares regression of
score on year. For everyone else: imagine the five yearly scores as
five dots on a graph, drawing a line that fits them best, and asking
whether the line goes up or down and how steeply.)

The slope is measured in **points per year on the 0–100 scale**:

- A slope of **+1.5** means "the score is rising by 1.5 points per
  year, so after a decade it will be 15 points higher."
- A slope of **−2.0** means "the score is falling by 2 points per
  year."

Based on the slope and volatility, every (country, module) gets
labeled with one of five **flags**:

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **improving** | Trend ≥ +1 point per year. Clearly moving up. |
| **deteriorating** | Trend ≤ −1 point per year. Clearly moving down. |
| **volatile** | No clear trend, but the score has been bouncing around (std dev > 5). |
| **stable** | Small or no movement, low volatility. |
| **insufficient_data** | Fewer than 3 years of data. Can't tell. |

Here is the USA's full trajectory summary:

```{r usa-trajectories}
trajectories |>
  filter(country_iso3 == "USA") |>
  arrange(desc(level)) |>
  select(country_iso3, module, latest_year, level, trend_5y, trend_10y,
         volatility_5y, flag) |>
  mutate(across(c(level, trend_5y, trend_10y, volatility_5y), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  kable(caption = "The United States' trajectory across all eight modules. 'level' is where the country is now; 'trend_5y' is how fast it has been moving over the last five years.")
```

This is the final compressed output: one summary row per country
per module, capturing where they are and where they're heading.

# B6. Recap — the three outputs

The pipeline produces three files on disk, mapping directly to sections
B1–B5:

| File | Produced by step | What's in it |
|---|---|---|
| `country_year_indicators.csv` | B1–B3 | Long panel: country, year, indicator, raw value, plus the two scaled columns (`pct_global`, `pct_fixed`). |
| `country_year_scores.csv` | B4 | Module composites: 8 modules × ~200 countries × 25 years. |
| `country_trajectories.csv` | B5 | One trajectory row per country per module. |

The indicator panel is intentionally slim — six columns. Indicator
metadata (which module, which unit, which source, direction) lives
once in `config/indicators.csv` rather than being repeated on every
row of the panel. The notebook joins on indicator metadata wherever
it's needed.

Sections **C1–C6** below explore these three files and ask whether
the picture they paint is reasonable.

---

# Part C — Exploring the world the data describes

This is where the rest of the notebook used to start. With the
groundwork in Parts A and B in place, we can now actually look at
the data and ask things like: is the coverage good? Do the
measurements make sense? What does the world look like in 2025?
Where is it heading?

# C1. What did we manage to collect?

This first section is a **stock-take**. Before drawing any
conclusions from the data, we want to know what is in it: which
indicators we successfully fetched, which years are well-covered,
and which countries have enough data to be reasoned about.

## C1.1 The complete indicator inventory

Here is every individual indicator the pipeline tracks, grouped by
module.

```{r indicator-table}
indicators |>
  arrange(module, indicator) |>
  select(module, indicator, source, unit, direction, weight, description) |>
  kable(caption = "Every indicator in the pipeline. 'direction' tells us which way is 'better' before scaling; 'source' tells us where the number originally came from; 'weight' tells us how much the indicator contributes to its module score (weights are renormalised per module).")
```

A quick sanity-check by source and module:

```{r source-module-summary}
indicators |>
  count(source, module) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = source, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(module) |>
  kable(caption = "How many indicators per module come from each source.")
```

A reader-friendly takeaway: the **rights** and **stability** modules
are both built almost entirely from V-Dem (via OWID), which means
they will be heavily correlated and effectively measure the same
underlying thing — political institutions. We'll see this directly
in **Section C3**.

## C1.2 Coverage at a glance

For each indicator, how many countries actually report a value in
each year? Sparse indicators carry less weight in scoring. The
right-edge fade in this heatmap is **reporting lag** — newer years
have less data because countries take time to publish their
statistics. That fade is *not* a meaningful trend in the world; it
is a fact about data freshness.

```{r coverage-heatmap, fig.height=10}
coverage_grid <- panel |>
  group_by(indicator, year) |>
  summarise(n_countries = n_distinct(country_iso3), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(indicators |> select(indicator, module), by = "indicator")

indicator_order_by_module <- indicators |>
  arrange(module, indicator) |>
  pull(indicator)
coverage_grid <- coverage_grid |>
  mutate(indicator = factor(indicator, levels = rev(indicator_order_by_module)))

ggplot(coverage_grid, aes(year, indicator, fill = n_countries)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = "Countries reporting") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(ANALYSIS_START_YEAR, max(panel$year), by = 5),
                     limits = c(ANALYSIS_START_YEAR - 0.5, max(panel$year) + 0.5),
                     expand  = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Data coverage: countries reporting each indicator, by year",
    subtitle = sprintf("Darker = more countries reporting that year. Right-edge fade = reporting lag, not a real trend. Window: %d–%d.",
                       ANALYSIS_START_YEAR, max(panel$year)),
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: World Bank API + OWID grapher exports"
  ) +
  theme_lp() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8))
```

**Reading this chart, plainly:**

- Each row is one indicator. Each column is one year.
- A dark cell means many countries reported that indicator in that
  year. A light cell means few countries did.
- Most economic and health indicators are dark across the whole
  window — they are well-collected and well-reported.
- The right edge of nearly every row fades to lighter — countries
  simply haven't filed their 2024 and 2025 numbers yet. This will
  affect *every* score we compute for the last 1–2 years and is one
  of the most important caveats in this whole notebook.
- A few rows are uniformly thin (sparse from left to right) — those
  indicators are weak inputs anywhere they appear.

## C1.3 Which countries are well-covered?

How complete is each country's data in the last five years? A
country with very few indicators reporting will have unreliable
module scores.

```{r country-completeness}
country_completeness <- panel |>
  filter(year >= latest_year - 5) |>
  group_by(country_iso3) |>
  summarise(
    indicators_present = n_distinct(indicator),
    indicators_total   = nrow(indicators),
    completeness       = indicators_present / indicators_total,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(country_completeness, aes(completeness)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "#1f77b4", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title    = "How many countries are well-covered?",
    subtitle = sprintf("Each country's share of indicators with any data in the last 5 years (out of %d total).",
                       nrow(indicators)),
    x = "Share of indicators with recent data",
    y = "Number of countries"
  ) +
  theme_lp()

cat(sprintf("Countries with at least 75%% coverage: %d\n",
            sum(country_completeness$completeness >= 0.75)))
cat(sprintf("Countries with less than 50%% coverage:  %d  (treat their scores as approximate)\n",
            sum(country_completeness$completeness < 0.50)))
```

**Reading this chart:** the horizontal axis is "fraction of all
indicators where this country has any recent data," and the bars
show how many countries fall in each bucket. The mass is on the
right — most countries are well-covered. But a long left tail of
small island states, recent conflict zones, and isolated countries
(North Korea, Eritrea, etc.) drops below 50% coverage. Their module
scores still exist in the output files, but every chart in this
notebook that ranks countries should be read with their thin
coverage in mind.

---

# C2. Are the inputs sane?

Before trusting any composite scores, we should sanity-check the raw
indicators themselves. Two failure modes destroy the whole pipeline:

1. **Extreme outliers** — one freakish value that distorts the
   min-max scaling for everyone else.
2. **Broken time series** — a sudden jump in a number that reflects
   a methodology change at the data source, not a real-world event.

This section surfaces them.

## C2.1 Distributions of each raw indicator

For each indicator, we draw a **boxplot** showing how the value is
distributed across all country-years. A boxplot is a compact summary
that shows the middle 50% of values as a box, the median as a line
inside, and "whiskers" reaching out to typical extremes.

The key thing to look for is indicators where the box is very thin
(values clustered close together) but the whiskers stretch a long
way (a few extreme outliers way out). Those are the indicators where
min-max scaling will compress 95% of countries into a narrow band
near 0.

```{r raw-distributions, fig.height=12}
panel_for_dist <- panel |>
  left_join(indicators |> select(indicator, module), by = "indicator") |>
  group_by(indicator) |>
  mutate(
    value_clip = pmin(pmax(value, quantile(value, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE)),
                                  quantile(value, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE))
  ) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(panel_for_dist, aes(x = value_clip, y = "")) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = module), outlier.size = 0.4, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ indicator, scales = "free_x", ncol = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = MODULE_COLORS, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of every indicator across all country-years",
    subtitle = "Clipped at 1st/99th percentiles so the display isn't dominated by outliers.",
    x = "Indicator value (clipped for display)", y = NULL,
    caption = "Use this to spot indicators whose raw distribution is so skewed that scaling collapses most countries near 0."
  ) +
  theme_lp() +
  theme(strip.text  = element_text(size = 8),
        axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

This is a wall of small charts on purpose — the goal is to scan it
quickly and spot indicators that look skewed.

## C2.2 The outlier diagnostic

A more focused look at the outlier problem. For each indicator we
compute the **ratio of the maximum value to the 95th-percentile
value**. A ratio of 1.2 is healthy (the maximum is a little higher
than the 95th percentile, like you'd expect from a normal-ish
distribution). A ratio of 50 means a tiny number of country-years
sit so far above the rest that they completely dominate the upper
range.

```{r outlier-check}
outlier_check <- panel |>
  group_by(indicator) |>
  summarise(
    p50 = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    p95 = quantile(value, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_over_p95 = max / p95,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(max_over_p95)) |>
  mutate(
    flag = case_when(
      max_over_p95 > 50 ~ "CRITICAL — log transform recommended",
      max_over_p95 > 10 ~ "watch — heavy tail",
      TRUE              ~ "ok"
    )
  )

outlier_check |>
  head(15) |>
  kable(digits = 2,
        caption = "The 15 indicators with the heaviest right tails. When max/p95 > 50, a small number of country-years swallow the entire upper range of the scaled scores.")
```

**What this is telling us, in plain language:** When you see "max
over p95 = 57," it means that the single largest value of this
indicator ever recorded is **57 times bigger** than the value at the
95th percentile (the value below which 95% of country-years fall).
That single freakish value becomes the "100" anchor of the all-time
scale, and everyone else gets crushed into the lower portion.

The confirmed bad cases in this run:

- **`co2_per_capita`** — the maximum is about 57× the 95th
  percentile. A handful of years in Gulf oil states recorded
  extraordinary per-person emissions, pulling every other country's
  climate score downward.
- **`inflation_cpi`** — the maximum is about 30× the 95th
  percentile. Hyperinflation episodes (Venezuela, Zimbabwe,
  Argentina, Sudan) make every other country's single-digit
  inflation look indistinguishable when scaled.
- **`mobile_subscriptions`** — reaches 574 subscriptions per 100
  people in one country-year (a tourist-roaming SIM-card artifact).
  The USA at ~120 per 100 people gets scaled to about 20 out of 100,
  which is meaningless.

**The fix**, which is not yet implemented in the pipeline, is to
apply a **logarithmic transformation** to these indicators before
scaling — that is, take the log of each value first, which pulls
the long tail back in. Or to **winsorize**, which means capping
values at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Either approach would
restore meaningful spread for the bulk of countries.

## C2.3 Suspect direction assignments

Recall that every indicator has a `direction` — either "higher is
better" or "lower is better" — that determines whether to flip its
score during scaling. Several indicators in this pipeline have a
direction encoded that doesn't survive careful scrutiny.

```{r direction-issues}
suspect <- tibble::tribble(
  ~indicator,                ~current_direction,  ~problem,
  "fertility_rate",          "higher_is_better",  "Not universal. High fertility with low resources isn't unambiguously better.",
  "population_growth",       "higher_is_better",  "Descriptive, not normative. Many wealthy countries have negative growth by choice.",
  "urban_population_share",  "higher_is_better",  "Debatable. Hyper-urbanization brings real social and environmental costs.",
  "trade_pct_gdp",           "higher_is_better",  "Openness vs vulnerability — context-dependent.",
  "gross_savings_pct_gdp",   "higher_is_better",  "Very high savings can signal weak domestic consumption.",
  "high_tech_exports_share", "higher_is_better",  "Rewards small specialised economies. Diverse manufacturers like the USA score poorly even though they lead in absolute high-tech output."
)
kable(suspect, caption = "Indicators whose 'direction' is arguable. Their contributions to module scores should be read with care.")
```

The most consequential case is the **demographics** module. Three
of its four core indicators are descriptive — they say something
about a country's population structure but don't carry an obvious
"better/worse" meaning. Encoding them as "higher is better" turns
them into noise rather than signal. We will see this confirmed by
hard numbers in **Section C3.2**.

---

# C3. Do the modules hang together?

A module score is a weighted average of its indicators. For that
average to mean anything, the indicators inside the module need to
**actually measure related things**.

If two indicators in the same module move in opposite directions —
one going up when the other goes down — averaging them just
cancels them out, like trying to find someone's "general health"
by averaging their heart rate and their height. The result is a
number, but it doesn't represent anything coherent.

Similarly, if two indicators in **different** modules move almost
identically, those modules aren't actually capturing distinct
phenomena. They're double-counting.

## C3.1 Correlation between every pair of indicators

We measure how strongly two indicators move together with a number
called the **correlation coefficient**, abbreviated *r*. It ranges
from −1 to +1:

- **+1.0** = the two indicators move perfectly together (when one
  goes up, the other always does too).
- **0** = no relationship — knowing one tells you nothing about the
  other.
- **−1.0** = the two indicators move perfectly *opposite* (when one
  goes up, the other always goes down).

In real social data, values above 0.6 are considered "strongly
correlated" and below 0.3 "weak."

Here is the correlation between every pair of indicators in the
pipeline, drawn as a heatmap. Blue = positive correlation (move
together). Red = negative correlation (move opposite). White = no
relationship. Indicators are grouped by module, with thick black
lines marking the module boundaries.

```{r correlation-matrix, fig.width=11, fig.height=10}
latest_per_indicator <- normalized |>
  filter(year >= latest_year - 2) |>
  group_by(country_iso3, indicator) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

cor_wide <- latest_per_indicator |>
  select(country_iso3, indicator, pct_fixed) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicator, values_from = pct_fixed) |>
  select(-country_iso3)

indicator_order <- indicators |>
  arrange(module, indicator) |>
  pull(indicator)
indicator_order <- intersect(indicator_order, names(cor_wide))
cor_wide        <- cor_wide[, indicator_order]

cor_mat <- cor(cor_wide, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

cor_long <- as.data.frame(cor_mat) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("ind_x") |>
  pivot_longer(-ind_x, names_to = "ind_y", values_to = "r") |>
  mutate(
    ind_x = factor(ind_x, levels = indicator_order),
    ind_y = factor(ind_y, levels = rev(indicator_order))
  )

module_boundaries <- indicators |>
  filter(indicator %in% indicator_order) |>
  arrange(factor(indicator, levels = indicator_order)) |>
  mutate(rownum = row_number()) |>
  group_by(module) |>
  summarise(boundary = max(rownum) + 0.5, .groups = "drop") |>
  pull(boundary)
module_boundaries <- head(module_boundaries, -1)

ggplot(cor_long, aes(ind_x, ind_y, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = module_boundaries, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = length(indicator_order) - module_boundaries + 0.5,
             color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#b2182b", mid = "white", high = "#2166ac",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Correlation (r)") +
  labs(
    title    = "Indicator correlation matrix (latest year)",
    subtitle = "Indicators ordered by module (black lines = module boundaries).\nDark blue blocks along the diagonal = modules are internally consistent. Strong off-diagonal blocks = redundancy across modules.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_lp() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1, size = 7),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))
```

**Reading this heatmap:**

- Look at the **square blocks along the diagonal**, one per module.
  A module is "internally consistent" if its block is uniformly
  dark blue — its indicators all move together.
- Strong blue **outside the diagonal blocks** means two modules are
  measuring overlapping things.
- Any **red** cells flag pairs of indicators that move in opposite
  directions. If those two indicators are in the same module, the
  module's average is incoherent.

The most obvious feature in this run is the **strong blue block
where the rights module meets the stability module**. They are
almost the same data (V-Dem indices), so the modules are essentially
duplicating each other.

## C3.2 The module coherence summary

The heatmap is a lot to look at. Here is a single-number summary
per module: the average correlation between pairs of indicators
inside the module.

```{r within-module-coherence}
within_module_cor <- indicators |>
  group_by(module) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    inds <- intersect(.x$indicator, names(cor_wide))
    if (length(inds) < 2) return(tibble(avg_r = NA_real_, min_r = NA_real_, n_pairs = 0))
    sub <- cor_mat[inds, inds]
    sub[upper.tri(sub, diag = TRUE)] <- NA
    vals <- as.vector(sub)
    vals <- vals[!is.na(vals)]
    tibble(avg_r = mean(vals), min_r = min(vals), n_pairs = length(vals))
  }) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_r))

kable(within_module_cor, digits = 2,
      caption = "Average and minimum correlation among indicators within each module. Negative min_r means at least one indicator pair is moving in opposite directions inside the module.")
```

**Reading this table:**

- `avg_r` is the average correlation between every pair of
  indicators inside the module. Higher is better — it means the
  indicators agree with each other.
- `min_r` is the *worst* correlation — the most disagreeing pair.
  If this is below 0, then at least one indicator in the module is
  actively pulling against the others.

What we see in this run:

- **rights** (avg r ≈ 0.91) and **stability** (avg r ≈ 0.87) are
  *internally extremely coherent*. They are all V-Dem indices
  measuring closely related aspects of political institutions.
- **health, technology, labor, climate, economy** show moderate
  coherence. The weighted average is doing real work but the
  modules aren't measuring a single thing — they are reasonable
  thematic groupings of different but related measurements.
- **demographics** has an average correlation of about **−0.15**
  and a minimum pair correlation of about **−0.83**. Inside this
  module, indicators are *anti-correlated*. Averaging them
  produces a number that doesn't represent anything meaningful —
  it's pure statistical noise.

**Recommendation**: drop the `demographics` *score*. Keep its
indicators (they are useful individually as context — knowing a
country's age structure matters), but don't try to average them
into a composite. The composite is misleading.

---

# C4. What does the world look like right now?

Now that we have sanity-checked the inputs, we can finally look at
the headline output: what does each country's scorecard say at
present?

## C4.1 The shape of each module's scores worldwide

For each module, here is the **distribution of scores across all
countries** in the latest available year. The horizontal axis is
the score (0 = all-time global worst, 100 = all-time global best).
The vertical bars count how many countries fall in each bucket.

```{r score-distributions, fig.height=6}
latest_scores <- scores |>
  filter(year >= latest_year - 2) |>
  group_by(country_iso3, module) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(latest_scores, aes(score_pct_fixed, fill = module)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ module, ncol = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = MODULE_COLORS, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title    = sprintf("How module scores are distributed across countries (~%d)", latest_year),
    subtitle = "0 = matches all-time global worst on this module. 100 = matches all-time global best.\nA wide, even distribution = scoring is well-calibrated. A pile-up at 0 or 100 = outliers are distorting the scale.",
    x = "Module score (0–100)", y = "Number of countries"
  ) +
  theme_lp()
```

**Reading each panel:**

- **economy** has a thin tail stretching to the right with most
  countries crushed near 0–30. This is the visible footprint of the
  outlier problem from **C2.2** — Luxembourg and Qatar's per-person
  GDP sets a "100" anchor so high that everyone else looks bad.
- **climate** has a wide U-shape with a hump near 100. The hump is
  small, low-emission countries (poor countries) scoring full marks
  for not emitting much. This is the **"rewards poverty"** problem
  we'll see again in C4.2.
- **health** is heavily left-skewed near 75–85. Most countries are
  doing reasonably well on health. This is good news in the real
  world.
- **technology** is **bimodal** — two peaks rather than one. This
  is the digital divide showing up clearly: rich, digitally-connected
  countries cluster high, less-connected ones cluster low, and few
  countries are in between.
- **labor** clusters tightly around 70–80. The labor indicators
  don't discriminate much between countries — they are similar
  everywhere.
- **rights** and **stability** are roughly uniform — countries are
  spread fairly evenly from low to high. This is the **expected
  behavior** of a well-calibrated indicator. V-Dem is the most
  carefully constructed dataset in our pipeline and it shows.
- **demographics** is a tight bell curve around 50 — but as we
  established in C3.2, this is the *statistical ghost* of the
  module's anti-correlated indicators canceling each other out,
  not a meaningful signal.

## C4.2 Top 10 and Bottom 10 per module — the cheapest sanity check

If our scoring is working, the top 10 countries on rights should be
Scandinavian democracies. The top 10 on health should be wealthy
countries with strong healthcare systems. If something is broken
upstream, this is where it screams.

```{r top-bottom-table, fig.height=14}
top_bot <- latest_scores |>
  group_by(module) |>
  mutate(rank_top = rank(-score_pct_fixed), rank_bot = rank(score_pct_fixed)) |>
  filter(rank_top <= 10 | rank_bot <= 10) |>
  mutate(side = if_else(rank_top <= 10, "Top 10", "Bottom 10")) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(top_bot,
       aes(x = reorder(country_iso3, score_pct_fixed),
           y = score_pct_fixed, fill = coverage)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(side ~ module, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1,
                       limits = c(0, 1), name = "Data coverage") +
  labs(
    title    = "Top 10 and Bottom 10 per module (latest year)",
    subtitle = "Pale bars = thin coverage; the country's rank may reflect what's missing more than what's measured.",
    x = NULL, y = "Module score (0–100)"
  ) +
  theme_lp() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7),
        strip.text   = element_text(size = 8))
```

**This chart is the most informative diagnostic in the whole
notebook**, because it exposes specific problems. Reading the run:

- **Top 10 economy** includes countries like Afghanistan, South
  Sudan, Tonga, Uzbekistan, and Lebanon. These are obviously not
  strong economies. They score high because:
  - Low income inequality in a poor country rewards "no one is
    rich" rather than "people are doing well."
  - Tiny formal-sector economies have low measured unemployment
    (people are working informally, but that doesn't show up).
  - Sparse data lets a couple of favorable measurements dominate
    the average. The pale color bars confirm this — these are
    low-coverage countries.
  This is a **broken result** that the model is currently producing.
- **Top 10 climate** is Paraguay, Ethiopia, Nepal, São Tomé and
  Príncipe, Comoros, etc. These are countries with low per-person
  CO2 emissions because they are too poor to drive cars or run
  factories — *not* because they have decarbonized. **The climate
  module currently rewards poverty, not climate progress.** Adding
  measures like clean-energy share, energy efficiency, and forest
  cover would fix this.
- **Top 10 demographics** is dominated by Gulf states (UAE,
  Singapore, Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman) because
  migrant labor inflates their population growth rate, which the
  module currently treats as "higher is better." This is the
  direction-assignment problem from C2.3 in action.
- **Top 10 rights and stability** are Denmark, Switzerland, Norway,
  Sweden, Finland, Iceland, New Zealand, etc. — this looks right.
  It validates that the V-Dem-based modules are working.
- **Bottom 10 stability** includes Cambodia, Myanmar, Equatorial
  Guinea, Eritrea, Turkmenistan, Venezuela — also as expected.

The pattern is clear: **the V-Dem-based modules work; the others
have indicator-design problems that need to be fixed before their
scores can be trusted.**

## C4.3 The economy-vs-rights map (with caveats)

A two-dimensional scatter plot of countries on rights versus economy
is a classic way to visualize the regime-type landscape: rich
democracies in one corner, poor autocracies in another, and so on.

```{r economy-vs-rights, fig.height=7}
econ_rights <- latest_scores |>
  filter(module %in% c("economy", "rights")) |>
  select(country_iso3, module, score_pct_fixed) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = module, values_from = score_pct_fixed) |>
  filter(!is.na(economy), !is.na(rights))

to_label <- econ_rights |>
  filter(country_iso3 %in% c("USA","DEU","JPN","GBR","FRA","CAN","AUS","SWE","NOR",
                             "CHN","RUS","SAU","ARE","IRN","TUR","EGY",
                             "IND","BRA","ZAF","MEX","IDN","NGA",
                             "VEN","CUB","PRK","AFG","SOM","SYR",
                             "SGP","KOR","CHE","NLD"))

ggplot(econ_rights, aes(economy, rights)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50, color = "grey80") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50, color = "grey80") +
  geom_point(color = "grey60", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = to_label, color = "#1f77b4", size = 2.5) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = to_label, aes(label = country_iso3),
                           size = 3, max.overlaps = 50, segment.color = "grey70") +
  labs(
    title    = sprintf("Economy vs. Rights (~%d)", latest_year),
    subtitle = "The vertical axis (rights, from V-Dem) is reliable.\nThe horizontal axis (economy composite) is currently distorted by outliers (see C2.2) — read it as showing structure, not a clean wealth ranking.",
    x = "Economy score (0–100) — currently distorted",
    y = "Rights score (0–100)"
  ) +
  theme_lp()
```

**How to read this:**

- Each dot is a country. Highlighted dots are countries we've
  labeled.
- The vertical axis (rights) is the V-Dem score and is reliable —
  countries higher up score better on civil and political rights.
- The horizontal axis (economy) is the composite economy score and
  is *currently miscalibrated* because of the outlier issues
  documented in C2.2 — so the absolute X-position should not be
  read as a wealth ranking. But the *structure* of the chart still
  separates regime types.
- The familiar pattern emerges: Scandinavian democracies in the top
  region; authoritarian regimes (China, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Iran)
  lower down; collapsed states (Afghanistan, Somalia, Syria,
  Venezuela) in the bottom corners.

---

# C5. Where is the world heading?

This is the section that pays off the whole pipeline. We have
scorecards. Now: **are the scorecards moving?**

## C5.1 Global trend, one line per module

For each module, we plot the **median country's score** every year
from 2000 to today, with a shaded band showing the middle 50% of
countries (between the 25th and 75th percentile). This shows whether
the typical country is improving, stagnating, or declining on each
dimension — and how much variation there is.

```{r global-trends}
global_trend <- scores |>
  group_by(module, year) |>
  summarise(
    median = median(score_pct_fixed, na.rm = TRUE),
    p25    = quantile(score_pct_fixed, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    p75    = quantile(score_pct_fixed, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    n      = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 50)  # exclude sparse years

ggplot(global_trend, aes(year, median, color = module, fill = module)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p25, ymax = p75), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ module, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(ANALYSIS_START_YEAR, max(global_trend$year)),
                     breaks = seq(ANALYSIS_START_YEAR, max(global_trend$year), by = 5)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = MODULE_COLORS, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = MODULE_COLORS, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title    = sprintf("Global trend per module, %d–%d", ANALYSIS_START_YEAR, max(global_trend$year)),
    subtitle = "Line = the median country's score each year. Shaded band = the middle 50%% of countries.\nA rising line means countries collectively have moved closer to the all-time global best.",
    x = NULL, y = "Median country score (0–100)"
  ) +
  theme_lp()
```

**This is the most important chart in the notebook. Reading it
plainly, module by module:**

- **health** — a clear rising line. Globally, people are living
  longer, infant mortality is falling, healthcare access is
  expanding. This is the biggest unambiguously positive trend in
  the dataset, and it matches everything we know from public-health
  reporting.
- **technology** — a clear rising line. Internet access, mobile
  phones, and (where measured) R&D investment have spread widely.
- **rights** — rises through about 2012, then *falls*. This is the
  data picking up what political scientists call the "democratic
  recession" — the worldwide retreat of democratic freedoms since
  the early 2010s.
- **stability** — same pattern as rights (because the modules share
  V-Dem indicators). Rule of law and corruption metrics have
  worsened on average.
- **climate** — a falling line. Because our climate module
  *rewards* low per-person emissions, a falling score means
  emissions per person are rising globally. This is correct
  directionally — developing countries are industrializing, raising
  their per-person emissions — but again, our climate module is
  currently rewarding poverty more than progress, so read with
  caution.
- **economy** — a declining median. **This is probably an
  artifact.** As Luxembourg and Qatar's per-person GDP keeps rising
  faster than everyone else's, the all-time global maximum keeps
  moving, and most countries' fixed-scale score drifts down even
  if their economy is genuinely improving. Re-running with
  log-transformed GDP would likely show a flat-or-rising trend.
- **labor** — fairly flat, with a small dip during 2020–2021 (the
  COVID labor-market disruption).
- **demographics** — moves around but isn't interpretable, for
  reasons covered in C3.2.

These lines are *medians*, so they are robust to a few extreme
countries but can mask divergence. If half the world is improving
on health and half is deteriorating, the median can stay flat. To
detect divergence, we look at the next chart.

## C5.2 How many countries are improving, deteriorating, or stable?

This chart applies the **trajectory flag** logic from Section B5
to every country in every module, then shows what fraction got each
label.

```{r trajectory-flag}
flag_dist <- trajectories |>
  filter(flag != "insufficient_data") |>
  count(module, flag) |>
  group_by(module) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(flag = factor(flag, levels = c("deteriorating", "volatile", "stable", "improving")))

ggplot(flag_dist, aes(module, share, fill = flag)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.75) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    deteriorating = "#b2182b",
    volatile      = "#d6604d",
    stable        = "#bdbdbd",
    improving     = "#2166ac"
  )) +
  labs(
    title    = "Share of countries by trajectory flag, in each module",
    subtitle = "Blue = improving (gaining >=1 pt/yr over the last 5 years). Red = deteriorating (losing >=1 pt/yr).\nGrey = stable. Pink = volatile (bouncing around but no clear trend).",
    x = NULL, y = "Share of countries", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_lp()
```

**This is the headline output of the world model.** From this run:

- **health**: about 85% of countries are improving. Almost no
  country is going backward on health.
- **technology**: a third are improving, a third are stable, and
  notably about a third are *deteriorating*. This last figure is
  almost certainly inflated by reporting lag — countries whose
  latest year is missing some technology indicators get a lower
  score for that year not because their tech got worse but
  because the *measurement* got thinner. **Don't trust the
  deteriorating share for technology in this run.**
- **rights** and **stability**: about 30% deteriorating versus
  about 12% improving. This is the **democratic backsliding
  finding** in our own data — and it is a robust finding because
  V-Dem coverage is good.
- **economy**: a confusing mix, partly because of the scaling
  problems documented in C2.2.
- **labor**: mostly stable.

## C5.3 "Level vs trend" — where countries are, and where they are going

For a single module at a time, this chart shows where each country
currently stands (horizontal axis) versus how fast it's moving
(vertical axis). It puts the two most important pieces of
information in one place.

```{r slope-level, fig.height=7}
plot_slope_level <- function(target_module) {
  d <- trajectories |>
    filter(module == target_module, !is.na(trend_5y), !is.na(level), n_years_5y >= 4)

  ggplot(d, aes(level, trend_5y)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 50, color = "grey60") +
    geom_point(aes(size = n_years_5y), color = MODULE_COLORS[[target_module]], alpha = 0.6) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
      data = d |> filter(country_iso3 %in% c("USA","CHN","IND","DEU","JPN","GBR","BRA",
                                             "RUS","ZAF","NGA","SAU","IRN","TUR",
                                             "MEX","IDN","KOR","FRA","ITA","CAN","AUS")),
      aes(label = country_iso3), size = 3, max.overlaps = 30
    ) +
    scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 4), guide = "none") +
    labs(
      title    = paste("Module:", target_module, "— level vs trend"),
      subtitle = "Horizontal: where the country stands now (0–100). Vertical: how fast it's moving (points per year over last 5 years).\nTop-right = high and rising. Bottom-left = low and falling. Top-left = low and catching up. Bottom-right = high but slipping.",
      x = "Latest level (0–100)",
      y = "5-year trend (points per year)"
    ) +
    theme_lp()
}

plot_slope_level("rights")
plot_slope_level("economy")
plot_slope_level("climate")
```

**How to read these:** the chart is divided into four quadrants by
the dotted lines at level=50 and trend=0.

- **Top-right (high level, rising)**: doing well and getting better.
  The "good news" quadrant.
- **Top-left (low level, rising)**: catching up. The "convergence"
  quadrant — a poor country making real gains.
- **Bottom-left (low level, falling)**: doing badly and getting
  worse. The "crisis" quadrant.
- **Bottom-right (high level, falling)**: established but slipping.
  This is the quadrant that contains most of the alarming
  democratic-backsliding stories.

For **rights**, this run shows established democracies (USA, France,
Germany, UK) clustered in the bottom-right quadrant — high level,
declining slope. That is the V-Dem democratic-recession finding
showing up directly in this notebook's own analysis.

For **economy**, treat the horizontal axis with the skepticism that
C2.2 demands.

For **climate**, the cluster at level near 100 with trend near 0 is
small low-emission countries — the "you can't fall off the floor"
effect again.
