# C6. Profile of a single country

This last section is a **template**. You set one variable —
`target_country` — to any country's ISO3 code, and the rest of the
section generates a focused profile.

```{r country-config}
target_country <- "USA"   # change to any ISO3 code: DEU, JPN, IND, BRA, NGA, ...
```

## C6.1 Where does `r target_country` stand on each module?

This chart compares `r target_country` to every other country in
the world, module by module. For each module, the **grey bar** shows
where the middle 80% of all countries fall (from the 10th to the
90th percentile), the **short grey tick** marks the global median,
and the **colored dot** is `r target_country`'s score.

A dot in the middle of the grey bar means `r target_country` is
about average. A dot to the right of the bar means it is in the
top 10% of the world. A dot to the left means it is in the bottom
10%.

```{r country-profile, fig.height=5}
country_latest <- latest_scores |>
  filter(country_iso3 == target_country)

global_summary <- latest_scores |>
  group_by(module) |>
  summarise(
    p10 = quantile(score_pct_fixed, 0.10, na.rm = TRUE),
    p50 = median(score_pct_fixed,     na.rm = TRUE),
    p90 = quantile(score_pct_fixed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

profile <- global_summary |>
  left_join(country_latest |> select(module, country_score = score_pct_fixed, coverage),
            by = "module")

ggplot(profile, aes(y = module)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = p10, xend = p90, yend = module), color = "grey75", linewidth = 4) +
  geom_point(aes(x = p50), color = "grey40", size = 3, shape = "|") +
  geom_point(aes(x = country_score, color = module), size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = MODULE_COLORS, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title    = paste(target_country, "— module profile"),
    subtitle = "Grey bar = the middle 80%% of countries (10th to 90th percentile). Tick mark = global median. Colored dot = this country.",
    x        = "Score (0–100)", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_lp()
```

## C6.2 How `r target_country` has moved over time

Each panel below shows one module's score for `r target_country`
across all years, with a dashed line showing the trend over the
last 5 years (the same trend that fed the trajectory flag).

```{r country-timeseries-good, fig.height=7}
country_ts <- scores |>
  filter(country_iso3 == target_country)

ggplot(country_ts, aes(year, score_pct_fixed)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = module), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(color = module), size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed",
              color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.5,
              data = ~ filter(.x, year >= latest_year - 5)) +
  facet_wrap(~ module, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(ANALYSIS_START_YEAR, max(country_ts$year))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = MODULE_COLORS, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title    = paste(target_country, "— all modules over time"),
    subtitle = "Solid line = year-by-year score. Dashed line = 5-year trend (the same one feeding the trajectory flag).",
    x        = NULL, y = "Module score (0–100)"
  ) +
  theme_lp()
```

A few common patterns to look for in any country's profile:

- A **steady rise** across most modules — the development story of
  a country pulling itself up over time.
- A **single steep drop in one module** — usually identifies a
  crisis (financial collapse, war, coup) localized to that domain.
- A **broad simultaneous dip in 2020–2021** — almost certainly the
  COVID pandemic.
- A **sharp cliff in the last 1–2 years** — almost always reporting
  lag, not a real event.

## C6.3 Diving into the weakest module

When a country scores low on a module, the natural next question is:
**why?** What's dragging the score down? This chart breaks the
lowest-scoring module into its individual indicators.

```{r country-weakest-module, fig.height=5}
weakest <- country_latest |> slice_min(score_pct_fixed, n = 1) |> pull(module)

drilldown <- normalized |>
  left_join(indicators |> select(indicator, module), by = "indicator") |>
  filter(country_iso3 == target_country,
         module == weakest,
         year >= latest_year - 2) |>
  group_by(indicator) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(pct_fixed)

ggplot(drilldown, aes(x = pct_fixed, y = reorder(indicator, pct_fixed))) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = 50, yend = indicator), color = "grey80") +
  geom_point(aes(color = pct_fixed < 50), size = 4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f", pct_fixed)),
            hjust = -0.4, size = 3.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#b2182b", `FALSE` = "#2166ac"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 105)) +
  labs(
    title    = paste(target_country, "— indicator breakdown for weakest module:", weakest),
    subtitle = "Each dot is one indicator's score on the all-time global scale. Red = below global midpoint of 50. Blue = above.",
    x        = "Indicator score (0–100)",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_lp()
```

This drill-down is the most useful diagnostic tool when a module
score surprises you. **Worked example: the USA's technology module
in this run** — the country comes out with a mediocre technology
score, which is counter-intuitive. Drilling in shows:

- `internet_users_share = 93` (very high — sane).
- `rd_expenditure_pct_gdp = 54` (around average — sane).
- `mobile_subscriptions = 20` (USA at about 120 per 100 people, but
  the all-time global maximum is 574 — see C2.2 — so the USA gets
  unfairly scaled to 20).
- `high_tech_exports_share = 25` (USA exports enormous absolute
  volumes of high-tech goods, but they're a small *share* of its
  diverse manufacturing mix — see C2.3; this is the wrong proxy
  for tech leadership in large economies).

So the USA's "low" technology module score is **not a real signal
about US technological capability**. It is the model's broken
indicators showing up. Looking at the indicator-by-indicator
breakdown is the only way to catch this.

## C6.4 Comparing with peer countries

Lastly, how does `r target_country` compare to a chosen peer group
on its weakest module?

```{r peer-comparison, fig.height=5}
peers <- c("USA", "DEU", "JPN", "GBR", "FRA", "CAN", "AUS")  # edit as desired
peer_module <- weakest

scores |>
  filter(country_iso3 %in% peers, module == peer_module) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, score_pct_fixed, color = country_iso3)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(ANALYSIS_START_YEAR, latest_year)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title    = paste("Peer comparison —", peer_module, "module"),
    subtitle = "If all peer countries show a sharp drop in the last 1–2 years on the same module,\nthat almost certainly reflects reporting lag, not a real event.",
    x = NULL, y = "Module score (0–100)"
  ) +
  theme_lp()
```

**An important interpretive note.** If every peer country shows a
sharp drop in the last 1–2 years on the same module, that is
almost certainly a **reporting-lag artifact** — half the
indicators stopped updating before the others, so the latest score
is computed from a smaller and different subset than prior years.
The `coverage` column on the score table records this
explicitly. In the technology peer-comparison from this run, all
G7 countries drop from about 50 to about 25 in the last two years
— that drop is *not real*, and the trajectory flag for those
countries on technology is contaminated by it.

---

# Part D — What this model cannot do

A careful reader at this point should feel two things:

1. The pipeline is **doing real work**. The V-Dem-based modules are
   producing reasonable rankings and capturing real-world trends
   (democratic backsliding). The health module is picking up the
   genuine global improvement in longevity and child survival.
2. The pipeline is **not finished**. Several modules have known
   bugs that produce technically-correct but misleading numbers.

This section is honest about both.

# D1. Known active issues in this run

These are bugs the diagnostics in Parts B and C have already
surfaced. They are listed here in roughly the order they should be
fixed.

| Issue | Where it lives | What it would take to fix |
|---|---|---|
| OWID datasets contain data going back to 1789, which is included in the scaling range. | OWID fetch and combine scripts. | Restrict the date range either at fetch time or right after loading. The notebook currently filters defensively. |
| Min-max scaling crushes most countries on heavy-tailed indicators (CO2, inflation, mobile subscriptions). | `helpers.R::normalize_indicators`. | Add a `transform` column to `indicators.csv` (values: `none`, `log`, `winsorize`) and respect it during scaling. |
| The economy module rewards small, poor countries with sparse data. | Indicator choices + outlier-driven scaling. | Same as above, plus reconsider whether low income inequality should be rewarded in low-wealth contexts. |
| Demographics indicators are anti-correlated within the module. | Module composition. | Drop the `demographics` *score*. Keep the indicators as context. |
| `mobile_subscriptions` has a 574-per-100 outlier (Macau / Hong Kong tourist roaming). | Raw World Bank data. | Winsorize during the scaling step. |
| `high_tech_exports_share` rewards specialization, not capability. Large, diversified manufacturers like the USA score poorly. | Indicator choice. | Replace with absolute R&D spending in PPP terms or patents per capita. |
| Trajectory flag is contaminated by reporting lag. | `helpers.R::compute_trajectories`. | Either require coverage to be stable across the 5-year window, or compute trends only on a fixed indicator subset. |
| `rights` and `stability` modules are highly redundant (both are V-Dem). | Module design. | Merge them into a single `governance` module, or add a true stability source (UCDP conflict data) to differentiate them. |

Most of these fixes are small and localized. None of them require
re-architecting the pipeline.

# D2. What this model is not equipped to do at all

The original framing of the project mentioned three eventual steps:
build a world model (Step 1), predict future trends (Step 2), and
project individual life paths (Step 3). This notebook is part of
Step 1. The other two are **substantially out of reach** with the
current setup, and being honest about why is important.

## D2.1 Why this is not a forecast

This is a **descriptive** model, not a predictive one. It tells you
where countries are and where they have recently been. It does not
say where they are going next year.

To do real forecasting, several things would have to change:

- The trajectory flag is just a straight line drawn through the
  last five years. That is fine as a description. It is not a
  prediction — straight lines extrapolated forward almost never
  match what actually happens.
- Real time-series forecasting uses models that can capture
  non-linear movement, sudden shocks, and uncertainty bands
  (techniques with names like ARIMA and state-space models). None
  of those are used here.
- All of our current indicators are *lagging* — they report what
  has already happened. Real prediction needs *leading* indicators
  — early signs of change. We don't have those.
- We have no event data. Wars, coups, financial crises, and
  pandemics are absent from our inputs. They are the most important
  things to predict. UCDP and EM-DAT would help.
- We don't model how countries affect each other. A recession in
  China is not independent from one in South Korea. Our trajectory
  computation treats each country in isolation.

## D2.2 Why this cannot project individual life paths

Country-level scorecards are **priors** on individual outcomes, not
predictions of them. Knowing a country has good healthcare on
average doesn't tell you whether *one particular person* will get
good healthcare; it just shifts the odds.

To go from country-level scorecards to a usable picture of how an
individual life might unfold, you would additionally need:

- Distributions of individual outcomes *within* each country —
  what fraction of people achieve a given income, education, life
  expectancy, etc. Datasets like the Demographic and Health
  Surveys, the Gallup World Poll, and OECD's Better Life Index
  contain this.
- A probabilistic framework that maps country-level inputs to
  individual-outcome distributions, with the right uncertainty
  attached.
- Honesty that the output is then **a range of informed scenarios,
  not predictions**. There is no responsible way to tell an
  individual person what will happen to them based on
  country-level data alone.

# D3. The trustworthy parts

Despite the caveats above, several parts of this pipeline are
trustworthy *as descriptive instruments*:

- **The V-Dem-based modules (`rights` and `stability`)** are
  producing rankings that match well-established findings in
  political science. The democratic-backsliding trend visible in
  this notebook's own data is consistent with how V-Dem itself
  reports it.
- **The health module** captures the long, robust global trend of
  improving life expectancy and falling infant mortality.
- **The data infrastructure** — the panel, the coverage tracking,
  the trajectory summary — is solid. The bugs are in indicator
  selection and scaling, not in the structure.

That structure is the foundation for everything else. Once the
indicator-level fixes in D1 are made, the rest of the pipeline does
not need to change.

# E2. Glossary

For the non-technical reader, the small set of terms used in this
notebook:

- **Country panel / panel data** — A table where every row is a
  combination of a country and a year (and possibly a measurement).
- **Indicator** — One specific measurable thing about a country
  (life expectancy, GDP per person, etc.).
- **Module** — A grouping of related indicators into a thematic
  scorecard subject (economy, health, rights, etc.).
- **ISO3 code** — The standard three-letter code for a country
  (USA, DEU, JPN, …). Used everywhere instead of country names to
  avoid mismatches.
- **`pct_global`** — A score 0–100 saying where a country ranks
  against others *this year* on one indicator. 50 = exactly the
  median country.
- **`pct_fixed`** — A score 0–100 saying where a country sits on
  the *all-time global scale* for one indicator. 0 = matches the
  all-time global worst, 100 = matches the all-time global best.
- **Direction** — Whether the original indicator is "higher is
  better" (like life expectancy) or "lower is better" (like infant
  mortality). After scaling, we flip the lower-is-better ones so
  higher = better everywhere.
- **Weighted average** — An average where some inputs count more
  than others. Used to combine an indicator's scores into a module
  score.
- **Coverage** — The share of a module's expected indicators that
  are actually available for a given country-year. Low coverage
  means the score is computed from less information.
- **Trend (5-year)** — The slope of the line that best fits the
  last five years of scores. Measured in points per year.
- **Volatility** — How much the score is bouncing around year-to-year,
  measured as the standard deviation over the last five years.
- **Flag** — One of `improving`, `deteriorating`, `volatile`,
  `stable`, or `insufficient_data`, summarising the trajectory.
- **Correlation (r)** — A number from −1 to +1 measuring how
  closely two indicators move together. +1 = perfectly together,
  0 = unrelated, −1 = perfectly opposite.
- **Outlier** — A single extreme value sitting far away from the
  rest of the data. Outliers are dangerous for min-max scaling
  because they anchor the upper limit far away from where most
  countries actually are.
- **Reporting lag** — The simple fact that countries publish their
  statistics with a delay, so the most recent 1–2 years always
  look thinner than older years.

# E3. Where to look first if something looks wrong

The pipeline writes a small text file at
`data/output/quality_report.txt`. It is generated automatically
every time the processing scripts run, and it records sanity-check
results (no duplicates, no bad years, no out-of-bounds scaled
values, sufficient country coverage, etc.). If any chart in this
notebook looks broken, that text file is the first place to look.
